messages.subject: Odd R2 using procD.pgls
parts:
Hi All,

I'm trying to use procD.pgls and I'm getting what I think is an odd result.

My tree has one tip per species and my data has several individuals landmarked per species. Therefore, I made mean shapes for each species from their procrustes aligned coordinates and similarly calculated the mean centroid size per species (CS was then log-transformed).  Then I popped these in a geomorph data frame with a groupings factor (group). I've triple checked the names are the same for each, the factor levels are correctly aligned to each species etc etc.. Then:

procD.pgls(shape~CS*group, phy, iter = 999, effect.type = "F", data = phylo_gdf)

And I get:
             Df      SS        MS        Rsq          F               Z         Pr(>F)  
CS           1    1017.59 1017.59  0.99808    9026.2781 3.4026  0.001 **
group        2    0.05      0.03       0.00005    0.2361      3.5050  0.022 *
CS:group   2    1.00     0.50       0.00098     4.4385      5.8630  0.002 **
Residuals  8    0.90     0.11       0.00088                          
Total         13 1019.54  

This is the table without phlyogenetic correction (with all the individuals across spp.) from the call  procD.lm(shape~CS*group, data = DF1):

              Df       SS       MS     Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)  
CS          1      0.021933 0.021933 0.07769 14.7722 3.7483  0.001 **
group        2     0.068804 0.034402 0.24371 23.1704 6.0348  0.001 **
CS:group   2    0.017872 0.008936 0.06330  6.0184 4.5136  0.001 **
Residuals 117  0.173716 0.001485 0.61530                        
Total     122 0.282325                                         


So, should I be using the mean shape? Is there something I'm missing completely?

Thanks,
Charles

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Odd R2 using procD.pgls
parts:
Charles,

 

That is hard to trouble shoot, though having an R2 of 0.998 for CSize is rather suspicious. The comparison you made though is uncontrolled because different datasets are used. I would first look at a nonphylogenetic analysis using the same data as in the PGLS analysis (ie, use procD.lm).  If you have similar R2 for CSize, then one of two things is possible.

 

One: you have crazy-different sizes across species and these are perfectly correlated with their average shapes.

 

Two: something in your procedures of obtaining average shapes, average sizes, or both is incorrect, causing a spurious and very high R2. 

 

I suggest you investigate via the non-PGLS approach first and then check all of your pre-analysis computations of averages.

 

Dean

parts:
Hi Dean,

Thanks for getting back to me.

Of course you are absolutely right regarding the comparison. Here is the table for the same mean shapes and mean sizes with OLS as in procD.lm:
Df        SS        MS     Rsq      F        Z Pr(>F)

CS         1 0.0051021 0.0051021 0.21885 3.0064  1.52237  0.030 *
group      2 0.0040948 0.0020474 0.17565 1.2064  0.92331  0.188 
CS:group    2 0.0005394 0.0002697 0.02314 0.1589 -1.80379  0.955 
Residuals  8 0.0135767 0.0016971 0.58236                        
Total     13 0.0233130

To get the mean shapes for species that appear on a tree I wrote a small function:
function(x,y){
  myList = list()
  for (i in 1:length(y$tip.label)){
    myList[[i]] <- mshape(x[,,which(dimnames(x)[[3]]==y$tip.label[i])])
  }
  names(myList)=y$tip.label
  myArray = abind(myList, along=3)
  return(myArray)
}

where y is a tree, and x is an array with potentially many individuals from the same species that all share the same species name.

For the mean sizes I just did: CS_means = tapply(CS, names(CS), mean) . Again, ensuring the names were all the same species name for each individual.


If you can spot/suggest anything I'd be very grateful.

Best wishes,
Charles

parts:
Most interesting Charles.  So for shape ~ Csize, a non-phylogenetic regression has a relatively low R2 for CSize, but for the same data it is nearly 1.0 when doing phylogenetic regression. I have not seen a dataset quite that extreme in its difference before.

 

This, to me leads to two more options. One is that there is something odd with your tree, and the other is that both size and shape are extremely highly correlated with your tree, leading to the high association in the PGLS. The latter can be investigated by evaluating the phylogenetic signal in size, and in shape. The former, by investigating the tree.

Dean

parts:
Charles,

Is it possible that with your function to obtain mean shapes by species names (tip.labels), in one case (GLS) you accidentally used raw landmark coordinates for the x argument in your function?  Such a huge effect - association of CS and shape - suggests that the coordinates were not adjusted to be the same size via GPA.  This would be especially true if one specimen (at least) was large compared to some others.  Below is an example for how such a thing could manifest, and see how it looks similar to your example.

Cheers!
Mike

> data("plethspecies")
> plethspecies$land[,,1] <- plethspecies$land[,,1] * 10 # make one really large specimen
> Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)
  |======================================================| 100%
> gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(land = plethspecies$land, Csize = Y.gpa$Csize)
> fit <- procD.pgls(land ~ Csize, phy = plethspecies$phy, data = gdf)

Sums of Squares calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |=====================================================================| 100%
> summary(fit)

Call:
procD.pgls(f1 = land ~ Csize, phy = plethspecies$phy, data = gdf)

Randomized Residual Permutation Procedure Used
1000 Permutations

Residuals  7 0.0004 0.0001 0.00006                        
Total      8 7.1742

Hi Mike,

I didn't get back to you about this - but might be useful for others. The issue was caused by some very short edges on my tree (Dean pointed out it could be a tree issue before). I seem to have solved it by rescaling the edge lengths using the chronos function in ape.

Cheers,
Charles
On Saturday, September 22, 2018 at 8:13:35 PM UTC+1, Michael Collyer wrote:

Charles,

Is it possible that with your function to obtain mean shapes by species names (tip.labels), in one case (GLS) you accidentally used raw landmark coordinates for the x argument in your function?  Such a huge effect - association of CS and shape - suggests that the coordinates were not adjusted to be the same size via GPA.  This would be especially true if one specimen (at least) was large compared to some others.  Below is an example for how such a thing could manifest, and see how it looks similar to your example.

Cheers!
Mike

> data("plethspecies")
> plethspecies$land[,,1] <- plethspecies$land[,,1] * 10 # make one really large specimen
> Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)
  |======================================================| 100%
> gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(land = plethspecies$land, Csize = Y.gpa$Csize)
> fit <- procD.pgls(land ~ Csize, phy = plethspecies$phy, data = gdf)

Sums of Squares calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |=====================================================================| 100%
> summary(fit)

Call:
procD.pgls(f1 = land ~ Csize, phy = plethspecies$phy, data = gdf)

Type I (Sequential) Sums of Squares and Cross-products
Randomized Residual Permutation Procedure Used
1000 Permutations
ANOVA effect sizes and P-values based on empirical F distributions


          Df     SS     MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)   
Csize      1 7.1737 7.1737 0.99994 113923 4.7315  0.001 **
Residuals  7 0.0004 0.0001 0.00006                        
Total      8 7.1742                                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
On Sep 22, 2018, at 11:53 AM, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

Most interesting Charles.  So for shape ~ Csize, a non-phylogenetic regression has a relatively low R2 for CSize, but for the same data it is nearly 1.0 when doing phylogenetic regression. I have not seen a dataset quite that extreme in its difference before.
 
This, to me leads to two more options. One is that there is something odd with your tree, and the other is that both size and shape are extremely highly correlated with your tree, leading to the high association in the PGLS. The latter can be investigated by evaluating the phylogenetic signal in size, and in shape. The former, by investigating the tree.
 
Dean

Hi Dean,
 
Thanks for getting back to me. 
 
Of course you are absolutely right regarding the comparison. Here is the table for the same mean shapes and mean sizes with OLS as in procD.lm:
 
          Df        SS        MS     Rsq      F        Z Pr(>F)  
CS         1 0.0051021 0.0051021 0.21885 3.0064  1.52237  0.030 *
group      2 0.0040948 0.0020474 0.17565 1.2064  0.92331  0.188  
CS:group    2 0.0005394 0.0002697 0.02314 0.1589 -1.80379  0.955  
Residuals  8 0.0135767 0.0016971 0.58236                         
Total     13 0.0233130 
 
To get the mean shapes for species that appear on a tree I wrote a small function:
function(x,y){ 
  myList = list()
  for (i in 1:length(y$tip.label)){
    myList[[i]] <- mshape(x[,,which(dimnames(x)[[3]]==y$tip.label[i])])
  }
  names(myList)=y$tip.label
  myArray = abind(myList, along=3)
  return(myArray)
}
 
where y is a tree, and x is an array with potentially many individuals from the same species that all share the same species name.
 
For the mean sizes I just did: CS_means = tapply(CS, names(CS), mean) . Again, ensuring the names were all the same species name for each individual.
 
 
If you can spot/suggest anything I'd be very grateful.
 
Best wishes, 
Charles 
 
 
On Friday, September 21, 2018 at 9:28:39 PM UTC+1, Dean Adams wrote:

Charles,
 
That is hard to trouble shoot, though having an R2 of 0.998 for CSize is rather suspicious. The comparison you made though is uncontrolled because different datasets are used. I would first look at a nonphylogenetic analysis using the same data as in the PGLS analysis (ie, use procD.lm).  If you have similar R2 for CSize, then one of two things is possible.
 
One: you have crazy-different sizes across species and these are perfectly correlated with their average shapes. 
 
Two: something in your procedures of obtaining average shapes, average sizes, or both is incorrect, causing a spurious and very high R2.  
 
I suggest you investigate via the non-PGLS approach first and then check all of your pre-analysis computations of averages. 
 
Dean

Hi All,
 
I'm trying to use procD.pgls and I'm getting what I think is an odd result.
 
My tree has one tip per species and my data has several individuals landmarked per species. Therefore, I made mean shapes for each species from their procrustes aligned coordinates and similarly calculated the mean centroid size per species (CS was then log-transformed).  Then I popped these in a geomorph data frame with a groupings factor (group). I've triple checked the names are the same for each, the factor levels are correctly aligned to each species etc etc.. Then:
 
procD.pgls(shape~CS*group, phy, iter = 999, effect.type = "F", data = phylo_gdf)
 
And I get:
             Df      SS        MS        Rsq          F               Z         Pr(>F)   
CS           1    1017.59 1017.59  0.99808    9026.2781 3.4026  0.001 **
group        2    0.05      0.03       0.00005    0.2361      3.5050  0.022 * 
CS:group   2    1.00     0.50       0.00098     4.4385      5.8630  0.002 **
Residuals  8    0.90     0.11       0.00088                           
Total         13 1019.54  
 
This is the table without phlyogenetic correction (with all the individuals across spp.) from the call  procD.lm(shape~CS*group, data = DF1):

              Df       SS       MS     Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)   
CS          1      0.021933 0.021933 0.07769 14.7722 3.7483  0.001 **
group        2     0.068804 0.034402 0.24371 23.1704 6.0348  0.001 **
CS:group   2    0.017872 0.008936 0.06330  6.0184 4.5136  0.001 **
Residuals 117  0.173716 0.001485 0.61530                         
Total     122 0.282325                                          
 
 
So, should I be using the mean shape? Is there something I'm missing completely?
 
Thanks,
Charles
